name: Bolo tie

lead: A bolo tie is a braided cord or leather strip held at the throat by an ornamental slide, finished with metal tips. It gives the neckline a deliberate accent without a knotted necktie.
People wear it as a style statement: a silver or turquoise slide draws the eye to the collar and chest. It is associated with Western wear and has seen periodic fashion revivals.

paras: It is worn around a buttoned collared shirt, with the slide moved up for a dressier look or lower for a casual one. Slide design, cord colour and the shirt it is paired with set the tone.
No health risks beyond ordinary clothing. Cord ends can catch on machinery, and leather cords are kept dry to avoid stiffening.

angle.text: Wearers use bolo ties to replace a conventional necktie with something more individual. The slide draws attention to the neck and chest area and signals a Western or vintage style.

lead: A bolo tie, also called a bola or shoestring tie, is a necktie made of cord or braided leather with decorative metal tips and an ornamental clasp or slide.[1] People use it to add a distinctive accessory at the neckline, which can make a plain shirt look intentional and frame the face.

Victor Cedarstaff of Wickenburg, Arizona claims to have invented it in the late 1940s and patented his slide design in 1959. Silver and turquoise slides are also part of Hopi, Navajo, Zuni and Pueblo silversmithing.[1]

paras: A bolo tie consists of a cord, an adjustable slide and metal tips; cords are commonly about 36 to 42 inches long and made of leather or braided material, and slides may be inlaid with turquoise or coral.[2]

Wikipedia reports that Cedarstaff filed his slide patent on May 24, 1954 and it was issued on July 28, 1959. Arizona made the bolo tie its official neckwear on April 22, 1971; New Mexico followed in 2007 and Texas also named it an official tie that year.[1] In the UK the style is called a bootlace tie and was worn by Teddy Boys in the 1950s, and it was fashionable again in the 1980s.[1] In 2013 and 2014 NFL quarterback Philip Rivers drew media attention for wearing them.[1]
It appears occasionally in style discussion as a way to add character to an outfit; forum mentions found are passing references rather than dedicated threads.

timeline.event: Cedarstaff claims to invent the bolo tie.[1]
Arizona adopts it as official neckwear.[1]
New Mexico makes it the official state tie.[1]
